paragraphs.heading: The bottom of the ocean
paragraphs.text: The seabed is simply the floor of the ocean. People also call it the seafloor, the sea floor, the ocean floor or the ocean bottom. Its large-scale shape across the whole global ocean is set by plate tectonics. Most of it, in oceans all over the world, lies under layers of marine sediment.

paragraphs.heading: From the coast to the deep
paragraphs.text: Heading out from a continent, the floor usually begins as a continental shelf. It then drops down the continental slope, a steep descent into deeper water. Where the slope meets the deep floor, the drop eases into the continental rise, which is built from sediment cascading down the slope. Beyond it lies the abyssal plain, the main area of the seabed. Most of the ocean is very deep, and that is where the floor takes this form.

paragraphs.heading: Ridges, trenches and vents
paragraphs.text: Seafloor spreading raises mid-ocean ridges down the middle of the major ocean basins, where the floor stands a little higher than the plain around it. This mountainous rise runs through the middle of all the oceans, typically with a rift along it. Along the edges of tectonic plates lie oceanic trenches, which are deep valleys. Where plates pass over a hotspot, periodic eruptions build ridges of volcanic islands. In volcanic areas and in trenches, hydrothermal vents push very hot, high-pressure water and chemicals into the near-freezing water around them.

paragraphs.heading: Layers of depth
paragraphs.text: Deep ocean water is sorted into zones by depth, and each has its own typical salinity, pressure, temperature and life. The abyssal zone sits along the top of the abyssal plain, with its lower edge at about 6,000 m. Below it is the hadal zone, from 6,000 to 11,000 metres, which takes in the trenches and is the deepest zone of all. Depth measured down into the seabed itself, for example through a sediment core, is called depth below seafloor and is often written mbsf, for meters below the seafloor.

paragraphs.heading: Four kinds of sediment
paragraphs.text: Seabed sediments are grouped by where their material comes from. Terrigenous sediment comes from the continents, worn away by rain, rivers and glaciers or blown out to sea as dust and volcanic ash, and it is the most plentiful kind on the floor. Biogenous sediment is made of the hard parts of sea creatures, mainly phytoplankton. Hydrogenous sediment precipitates out of seawater when ocean conditions change, or forms in hydrothermal vent systems, while cosmogenous sediment comes from space. Sorted by size instead, sediment runs from fine clays and silts, together called mud, up through sand to boulders.

paragraphs.heading: A slow rain of shells
paragraphs.text: Living things help build the seabed. Phytoplankton with shells of silicate or calcium carbonate grow in great numbers near the surface. When they die, their shells sink to the floor and become part of its sediment. Microorganisms living inside the sediment also change the chemistry of the seabed.

paragraphs.heading: People and the seabed
paragraphs.text: To map the floor, ships use sound to measure water depths around the world, and submersibles help scientists study unusual seabed habitats like hydrothermal vents. People change the seabed too. Much of the world's plastic travels down waterways into the ocean, and some of it sinks to the bottom. Deep sea mining goes after valuable minerals in sulfide deposits, and dredging takes sand from shallow areas for construction and beach nourishment.
